name: The Five Phases
title: The Five Phases
answer: The Five Phases is a staged method for adopting an AI tool in a school: assess readiness, choose the pilot, set up governance, run and evaluate, and scale what works. Each phase ends with a deliverable and an owner, so leaders can see progress rather than rely on impressions. It matters because skipping a phase is the most common way a promising tool becomes an expensive disappointment.

sections.body: The idea is a sequence of five phases that turns an AI adoption from a single decision into a managed process. Each phase produces something a leader can hold in their hand, and Figure 4.2 lists the deliverable and owner for each one. The problem it solves is the common pattern where a promising tool is bought or launched without readiness, a clear pilot, governance, evaluation, or a plan for scaling. By making each step explicit, the method gives leaders checkpoints and accountability. It also allows the pace to match the risk, so low-stakes tools can move faster and high-stakes tools get more time.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or district, the work follows the five phases in order. The text says a small district can move through the first three phases in a month for a low risk tool such as a lesson planning assistant. A tool that touches student records or decisions about students deserves more time at every step. The text does not give grade bands, so the practical distinction is by stakes rather than by year group. The rule of thumb is that the higher the stakes, the slower the phases.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The supplied text gives no evidence label, study, figure, or finding for this idea. It refers to Figure 4.2 as a list of phases, deliverables, and owners, but that is a planning aid rather than research evidence. On the text provided, the Five Phases rests on practice rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The main limit is that skipping a phase is the most common way a promising tool turns into an expensive disappointment. The text also warns that tools touching student records or decisions about students deserve more time at every step, so speed is not a virtue when stakes are high. Each phase has an owner and a deliverable, which keeps decisions with named people rather than with the tool or the process. The text does not say that any phase removes human judgment, and the choice to scale what works remains a leadership decision. The higher the stakes, the slower the phases.
